articles.title: The GOP’s Enemy #1 for the Midterms: Socialism
articles.author: Ben Burgis
articles.content_excerpt: A very old joke imagines two elderly Jewish men sitting on a park bench. The first reads the local Yiddish-language newspaper. The second reads an antisemitic, pro-fascist paper. After a few minutes, the first turns to the second and asks, “How can you read that garbage?” The second replies, “When I read your paper, it’s nothing but bad news. It depresses me! When I read this paper, I hear that we run banks, the media, Hollywood. . . . It cheers me up!” I kept thinking of that yesterday as I watched the first night of the Republicans’ midterm “ convention ” (where no one was nominated, and no official business of any kind was conducted). articles.title: Found, But Not Rescued
articles.content_excerpt: In the middle of the ocean, a man was drowning. He could not hold fast to the ropes dangling from the bow and stern of the bulk carrier that stopped to help. Below, a small, blue wooden boat crammed with people was tossed by a raging storm. As high winds sloshed water over the deck, the passengers — who had sailed for a day and a night without drinking water — rushed toward the swaying ropes. But the lines slipped through their hands. The children lacked the strength to climb. Even for the strong, a single slip could mean being crushed beneath the swaying hull of the massive ship. “ We were all very scared in the moment and drove away from [the] big ship,” Daniel, a survivor from Eritrea, reportedly told rescuers, describing how the migrant boat he was on powered away from the larger vesse

articles.title: Train Crashes Destroyed Their Towns. Will Yours Be Next?
articles.content_excerpt: Nearly 10 years before the train derailment and subsequent chemical disaster in East Palestine, Ohio, the town of Lac-Mégantic, Quebec experienced one of the deadliest rail disasters in North America. On July 6 , 2013 , a runaway train derailed in the center of town, leveling buildings and dumping millions of tons of crude oil onto the surrounding area. 47 people were killed in the explosion. In July , Maximillian Alvarez and Dr. Nicole Fabricant sat down with a panel of guests from East Palestine and Lac-Mégantic to discuss what happens when your town becomes a sacrifice zone and how residents can join together to fight back against the corporations responsible. articles.title: In the Name of Security
articles.content_excerpt: When Karla Padilla started her sentence at the federal correctional institution in Dublin, Calif., in 2023 , a guard singled her out. Over the next 15 months, the guard strip-searched Padilla so frequently that anyone near her risked being searched too, and other inmates began keeping their distance whenever that guard was on shift. Most prisons across the country conduct strip searches under a federal policy that requires women officers to inspect incarcerated women. The officer instructs them to remove their clothes, shake their hair, open their mouths, lift their breasts or genital area and then bend, squat and cough. articles.title: Universities Are Teaching the Virtue of Overwork
articles.author: Nicholas Liu
articles.content_excerpt: Although the University of Chicago bears “Let knowledge grow from more to more; and so be human life enriched” as its official motto, a different slogan entirely has attained much wider fame. Thanks to long-cemented campus lore, the university is best known instead by the refrain of its student body: “Where fun goes to die.” The slogan is spoken in weary, ironic tones, suggesting a strange marriage of acceptance and self-congratulation. Yes, life can be miserable, and yes, the vigor of UChicago’s curriculum is exactly what I came here for, and it will not break me . articles.title: The Discreet Charm of John Berger
articles.author: John Livesey
articles.content_excerpt: Brits dislike intellectuals. But for much of the last century and the beginning of this one, John Berger proved himself a notable exception. Berger first achieved cult status during the 1970s thanks to the success of Ways of Seeing , a four-part BBC series exploring the history of Western art. The series was first broadcast at 10 p.m. on a Saturday night, just after the weekend football scores. And yet, despite this unfavorable programming slot, the show still managed to become a national sensation, electrifying viewers with its efforts to dismantle the “great man” theory of art and shed new light on the economic and political contexts in which European masters were produced. articles.title: Guerrilla Cinema
articles.content_excerpt: In 1969, Argentine filmmakers Octavio Getino and Fernando Solanas published “Toward a Third Cinema,” a manifesto that rejected both Hollywood spectacle (“first cinema”) and European art house auteurism (“second cinema”) in favor of something new: films made as acts of political struggle, screened clandestinely, and designed to turn spectators into participants. It became the theoretical spine of a movement that swept the decolonizing world. Here are five essential films from Third Cinema, the militant movement that turned filmmaking into anti-imperialist struggle. articles.title: How Brazilian Cinema Survived Fascism
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content_excerpt: When writer-director Kleber Mendonça Filho was on a press junket with his sensational genre-twisting, furiously satirical 2019 film, Bacurau, Brazilian cinema was in a state of crisis. Jair Bolsonaro’s oppressive right-wing government targeted the national cinema for destruction, aggressively slashing budgets, halting funding, canceling projects, and leaving thousands of films at various stages of development stuck in limbo. articles.title: Five Books About Imperialism
articles.author: Vivek Chibber
articles.content_excerpt: Marxist Theories of Imperialism: A Critical SurveyAnthony Brewer1980There is a wide range of literature theorizing imperialism, and the best place to start is an overview that is judicious, encompassing, and careful. Brewer’s book is that. It covers not only the classical theories of Vladimir Lenin and Rosa Luxemburg but also the postwar theories, like the unequal exchange arguments of Giovanni Arrighi, Immanuel Wallerstein, and Samir Amin and dependency theory. Brewer is good on all of these, laying out what each theory claims and subjecting it to serious critical scrutiny. Any socialist who reads this book will come away literate in the broad landscape of Marxist theorizing on empire.From Value to Uneven Development: Selected Writings by John Weeks in the Marxist TraditionJohn Weeks, ed.

articles.title: Agitslop
articles.content_excerpt: In 1872, George Crofutt, a publisher of travel guides advertising the American West, commissioned a painting from the German-born John Gast: an idyllic depiction of westward-bound American pioneers. Floating above them is Columbia, the female personification of the United States that inspired the following decade’s Statue of Liberty, bearing a textbook in one hand and a telegraph wire in the other. In her wake come the hallmarks of American modernization that would lend the painting its name: railroad, ships, and farmers, all illuminated by a rising sun marching inexorably westward across the sky. articles.title: Raphäel Glucksmann, a Hawk in Progressive Clothing
articles.author: Eldar Mamedov
articles.content_excerpt: On August 23, Raphaël Glucksmann, the French essayist and member of the European Parliament (MEP), officially announced what had long been an open secret: his candidacy for the 2027 presidential election as a standard-bearer of the French center left. To my eyes, his candidacy is a disaster in the making and, in fact, a story I’ve already seen unfold from close range. I first encountered him not in Paris elite circles but in the wreckage of Georgian hubris, back in 2013, when I visited that country as part of the delegation of the European Parliament’s foreign affairs committee. Glucksmann, then in his early thirties, was suave, articulate, and utterly convinced of his own righteousness.
